title: Blaise (3 February)
hook: a bishop who, in his story, saved a boy choking on a fishbone; throats are blessed with crossed candles

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angela Merici, who opened a third door for women and set them teaching. Your line was teach the girls.

Early February, a weekday Mass, and at the end a line forms at the front. One by one, people step up, and the priest holds two long candles, crossed in an X and tied with a ribbon, gently against each throat. A short blessing, and they step aside. Kids giggle at the candles under their chins. Older people close their eyes. Someone with a cold coughs and gets blessed anyway. It's a gentle, slightly strange custom, and it belongs to a bishop called Blaise.
screen: `A LINE AT THE FRONT OF CHURCH.` → `TWO CANDLES, CROSSED.` → `AGAINST EACH THROAT.`

segments.voice: Blaise was a bishop of Sebaste, in Armenia, in the early centuries, and he died a martyr. That much the Church remembers. The rest comes from later stories, and the Church tells them as stories. In the first, Blaise is being led away under arrest when a mother pushes through the crowd with her son. The boy has a fishbone stuck in his throat and can't breathe. Blaise blesses him and prays, and the bone comes loose. The boy lives. In the second, a poor woman's only pig has been carried off by a wolf, and at Blaise's word the wolf gives it back. Later, when Blaise is in prison, she comes to see him, bringing food and candles to light his cell. A throat, and candles: put them together and you get the custom. On his feast, a priest or deacon holds two crossed candles at each person's throat and asks God, through the prayers of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, to free them from illness of the throat and from every other illness. The candles are not magic; in Catholic teaching a blessing is a prayer, not a charm. It puts a whole body, the part that swallows and speaks and sings, into God's hands for a moment. The Church prays a line from the Psalms at the start of each day in the Liturgy of the Hours. In the Douay-Rheims: "O Lord, thou wilt open my lips: and my mouth shall declare thy praise." A throat, opened, for praise.
screen: `A BISHOP AND MARTYR OF SEBASTE.` · `A BOY WITH A FISHBONE.` · `A WOMAN BRINGS CANDLES TO HIS CELL.` · `A BLESSING IS A PRAYER, NOT A CHARM.` · then, large: `O LORD, THOU WILT OPEN MY LIPS.`

segments.voice: Notice your own throat for a moment, the swallow, the air moving through, then bring to mind someone whose throat hurts or whose voice is struggling: a friend with a cold, a teacher who's lost their voice, someone who finds it hard to swallow. If you pray, ask Saint Blaise to pray for them and say the psalm line, O Lord, open my lips; if you don't, wish them ease and a clear voice.
Blaise. A bishop and martyr of Sebaste. In his story he saved a boy choking on a fishbone, and on his feast throats are blessed with crossed candles.
Your line: the blessing of throats. Two crossed candles, one old story. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: On Saint Blaise's feast, Catholic parishes often offer the blessing of throats, with a priest or deacon holding two crossed candles at each person's throat while saying the blessing.

chat.says: Why did the priest put crossed candles on my throat today?
options: It's Saint Blaise's blessing: a prayer, not a charm, against illness of the throat.
It's an old way of checking for a fever before you receive Communion.
It marks the start of Lent, when every throat is blessed before fasting.
chat.meaning: In his story Blaise saved a boy choking on a fishbone and was brought candles in prison; the blessing is a prayer, not magic.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or emperor's name spoken. 'In the early centuries' is vague by design; tradition dates his death to the early fourth century. 'The rest comes from later stories' is a claim about sources; confirm or soften.

The blessing formula (through the intercession of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, may God deliver you from every disease of the throat and from every other illness) is the copyrighted modern English text; paraphrased, not quoted.
Candles for the blessing are often those blessed at Candlemas the day before; not stated in the voice.
Psalm 50:17 (Vulgate numbering) begins the Invitatory of the Liturgy of the Hours each day ('Lord, open my lips'). Confirm.
'The Church says plainly that a blessing is a prayer, not a charm': confirm against the Book of Blessings' general introduction.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Psalm 50:17 exactly.
